why: Duplicate of Hydrangea petiolaris, which is the same plant to a reader and to a nursery. Kept petiolaris because round 11 manifest names it (Ana, carried in the handoff since round 11). Note for the record: the botanically accepted name is Hydrangea anomala subsp. petiolaris, so the surviving row carries the subspecies epithet as if it were a species - a naming question, not a duplicate question, and left open deliberately.

plant.description: A vigorous climbing vine that attaches itself to walls and structures using aerial roots. In summer, it produces large flat clusters of white lace-cap flowers that are very attractive. The heart-shaped leaves turn yellow in autumn before dropping.
plant.water_needs: Regular watering during establishment and dry periods. Prefers consistent moisture but not waterlogged conditions.
plant.soil_needs: Prefers moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil. Tolerates a range of soil types but performs best with added organic matter.
plant.maintenance_notes: Prune after flowering to control size and remove dead or damaged growth. May take several years to establish and begin flowering. Tie in young stems until aerial roots develop.
plant.common_issues: Can be slow to establish and may take 3-5 years before flowering begins. Occasionally affected by aphids or powdery mildew in dry conditions.
plant.best_placement: North or east-facing walls, fences, or shaded structures where it can climb and spread.
plant.environment_benefits: Flowers provide nectar for pollinators including bees and beneficial insects during summer months.

seasonal_rhythm.autumn: Leaves turn yellow before dropping, revealing the attractive peeling bark on mature stems. The plant prepares for dormancy.
seasonal_rhythm.summer: Large flat clusters of white lace-cap flowers open from June through July, creating a spectacular display. The plant is at its most attractive during this period.
seasonal_rhythm.winter: Deciduous stems are bare, showing the cinnamon-brown peeling bark and aerial roots. The woody framework remains attached to its support structure.
seasonal_rhythm.late_spring: Foliage fills out fully creating dense coverage. Flower buds begin to form at the tips of stems in preparation for summer blooming.
seasonal_rhythm.late_summer: Flowers fade and foliage remains lush and green. The plant continues to grow and spread, producing new stems that will flower the following year.
seasonal_rhythm.early_spring: New growth emerges with fresh green leaves appearing on woody stems. The plant begins to put out new shoots and aerial roots for climbing.

plant.light_needs: Thrives in partial shade to full shade. Can tolerate some morning sun but prefers protection from hot afternoon sun.

seasonal_care.summer: Prune after flowering to control size and remove dead growth.
seasonal_care.early_spring: Tie in young stems to support until aerial roots develop.

plant.image_pick_reason: Shows a sharp, well-lit close-up of the distinctive sepal flower with fertile buds against a soft background, clearly identifying the species in bloom.

combinations.notes: Both thrive in partial shade with similar moisture needs, and the hosta's bold foliage complements the climbing hydrangea's delicate flowers.
The fern's lush green fronds provide a classic woodland texture beneath the climbing hydrangea in shaded areas.
The brunnera's spring blue flowers and heart-shaped leaves provide early interest before the hydrangea blooms in summer.
This shade-loving groundcover fills in below the climber and both tolerate similar cool, moist conditions.
Pairing two hydrangea species creates a cohesive cottage garden look with layered blooms in early to mid-summer.
